prompt: What's a problem that your generation solved that younger people don't appreciate?
chosen:
You know, I was just thinking about this the other day while I was out on a hike. I was talking to a friend who's a lot younger than me, and we were discussing the environment. She was saying how we're in such a crisis now, and how we're just now starting to wake up to the fact that we need to take care of the planet. And I was like, "Actually, we've been aware of this for a while now."

I remember when I was in high school, we were learning about the ozone layer and how it was being depleted by CFCs. We were taught about the importance of recycling and conserving energy. It was a big deal back then. And I think that's one of the things that's frustrating for me is that younger people seem to think that we're just now discovering all of this.

I mean, don't get me wrong, I'm glad that people are finally taking action and being more aware of the issues. But it feels like we're not giving ourselves enough credit for being ahead of the curve on some of these things. I think we're often portrayed as being lazy or apathetic, but that's not true. We were just as concerned about the environment as they are now.

And it's not just the environment. I think we also solved some big social issues, like the civil rights movement. I mean, we were the ones who were out protesting and fighting for equality. We were the ones who were pushing for change. And now, it feels like younger people are taking credit for it like it's their movement.

I'm not saying that I'm not happy to see people being passionate about these issues. I am. But I just wish we'd get some recognition for the work we did. We paved the way for a lot of the progress that's being made today.
rejected:
Mio dio, let me tell you, we solved so many problems back in my day. But one thing that comes to mind is how we managed to make ends meet on a tight budget. You see, my husband and I, we were young, just starting out, and we didn't have all these fancy credit cards and loans like they do now. No, no, no. We had to be careful with every penny.

I remember my mother, God rest her soul, she was a wise woman. She always said, "Save for a rainy day, cara." And we did. We saved and we budgeted, and we made sure we had enough for the essentials. We didn't have all these fancy gadgets and gizmos like they do now, but we were happy with what we had.

And you know what? We were more content, more satisfied with life. We didn't have all these expectations and entitlements like some of these young people do today. We worked hard, we earned what we had, and we were proud of it.

Now, I'm not saying it was easy. Oh no, there were struggles, there were hardships. But we persevered, we worked together as a family, and we made do. And that's something that I think is missing from today's youth. They're so focused on instant gratification, on getting what they want right now, without putting in the effort.

My husband and I, we raised our children on a budget, and they turned out just fine. They learned the value of hard work, of saving, of being responsible. And that's something that I think is essential for any young person to learn.
